summary: Describes a project to build a single-access-point service for searching for whitepages information on Swedish Internet users. It covers the technical infrastructure for directory gateways. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This was a plan to make one place to look up people in Sweden instead of many separate phone books.

subtitle: A gateway system that unifies directory searches across multiple Swedish service providers.

tldr.problem: Directory information in Sweden is spread across many independent service providers, each using different protocols and data formats. Users cannot search all providers from a single point.
tldr.mechanism: TISDAG defines a Directory Access Gateway (DAG) system with client-facing protocol converters (CAPs), a referral index, and service connectors (SAPs) that map queries across protocols and retrieve results from multiple providers.
tldr.outcome: The system provides a single-access-point whitepages service with uniform access regardless of the underlying provider's protocol, addressing all data equally.

facts.label: Service availability
facts.value: 7x24 (24 hours per day, 7 days per week)

today: RFC 2967 is Informational and describes a technical infrastructure project from October 2000. The TISDAG project and its successor systems informed later directory service development, though the project itself remains a Swedish infrastructure initiative rather than an Internet Standard.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
The TISDAG project aimed to solve a real-world problem: Swedish whitepages information was scattered across independent Whitepages Directory Service Providers (WDSPs), each managing their own data and speaking their own protocols. There was no single place to search.

The RFC defines a Directory Access Gateway (DAG) system that sits between end-users and the many providers. Instead of replicating all the data to one place (which WDSPs refused), TISDAG uses a clever approach: maintain only summary indexes from each provider, use those to find which providers might have the answer, then fetch the actual data from them when needed.
sections.eli5: Instead of copying everyone's phone books into one giant book, the system just keeps a list of who has which numbers. When someone searches, it looks up the list, finds the right book, and asks that book for the answer.

sections.title: The System Architecture
sections.content:
The DAG system has three main components. Client Access Points (DAG-CAPs) are protocol converters that accept queries in whatever protocol the end-user's software speaks: HTTP, SMTP, Whois++, LDAPv2, or LDAPv3. The CAP translates the query into the DAG's internal format (DAG/IP) and handles translating results back.

The Referral Index maintains summaries of what each WDSP has, built using the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP). When a CAP queries the index with a user's search terms, the index returns a list of which WDSPs might have matching records.

Service Access Points (DAG-SAPs) are the connectors to WDSPs. Each SAP understands one of the WDSP's native protocols (again, Whois++ or LDAP versions). When chaining is needed—that is, when the CAP must fulfill the query by contacting WDSPs directly—the SAP translates the internal query format into what the WDSP understands and translates results back.

All components communicate using DAG/IP, the internal protocol defined in Appendix C, ensuring that new protocols can be added without rebuilding the entire system.
sections.eli5: Three parts work together: doorkeepers (CAPs) let different software types ask questions, a file card catalog (the index) shows who has what, and go-betweens (SAPs) talk to the different phone book services.

sections.title: Queries and Data Formats
sections.content:
The DAG supports a specific set of query types: name alone, name with organization, name with locality, role with organization, and role with organization plus locality. Servers may match these using exact matches or substring matches, handling both case-sensitive and case-insensitive comparisons as appropriate.

All internal communications use UTF-8 encoding for character data, meeting modern internationalization needs. DAG-CAPs adapt to whatever character set their client protocol requires, but prefer UTF-8 when available.

The schema defined for the DAG is deliberately simple: the DAGPERSON schema carries information about people, and the DAGORGROLE schema carries information about organizational roles. Each WDSP's index is expressed using these schemas, and the CAPs and SAPs handle mappings to and from the native protocols' schemas. The Appendix B of the RFC defines canonical mappings for LDAP and Whois++ to keep inconsistencies at bay.
sections.eli5: The system lets people search by name, organization, location, or job title. Everything inside uses UTF-8 text, and each protocol gets translated between the simple internal format and what it needs.

sections.title: Query Processing and Referrals
sections.content:
When an end-user submits a query through a CAP, the system follows a straightforward path. First, the CAP translates the query into DAG/IP and asks the Referral Index which WDSPs might have matching records. For protocols that support referrals natively—Whois++ and LDAPv3—the CAP can pass those referrals back to the client, which then contacts the WDSPs directly.

For protocols without referral support, or when clients cannot handle referrals, the CAP performs query chaining. The CAP uses SAPs to contact each referred WDSP, translating the query into each WDSP's native protocol, gathering the results, and packaging them into a single response set for the client. This happens transparently—the client sees a single result set as if querying a single unified directory.

The system is designed to respond in a timely manner, no slower than typical web-server response times. Results can be pruned to avoid overwhelming clients with excessive hits, and error conditions (unrecognized queries, too many results) are handled appropriately for each protocol.
sections.eli5: The system finds the right phone books and either tells the client where to look directly, or goes and asks the phone books itself and brings back all the answers in one response.

sections.title: Security and Service Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC identifies two key security concerns. Information credibility requires that the data end-users see corresponds directly to what the WDSPs provided; the DAG must not corrupt or alter information in transit. Unauthorized access must be prevented; the RFC notes that further specifications would be needed for authentication and encryption if the service moved beyond public whitepages data.

WDSPs must commit to 7x24 availability to provide uniform access. They must provide their information through one of the standardized protocols (Whois++, LDAPv2, or LDAPv3) even if they prefer a different internal protocol. The system is designed to be non-preferential—results are presented fairly regardless of which WDSP provides them.

The architecture is modular enough that future protocols can be added without changing the core DAG-IP or Referral Index design. The specification assumes that a careful pilot deployment and operational experience would reveal any unforeseen issues.
sections.eli5: The data must be correct and unchanged as it passes through the system. The phone books promise to be always available. New ways of asking questions can be added later if needed.
